cosyn2025-tensor-polarization-options.title: Polarization options in inclusive DIS off tensor polarized deuteron
key_content: Eq. (10): exact spin-1 inclusive cross section for UNPOLARIZED electrons: dsigma/dxdQ2 = pi y^2 alpha^2/(Q^4(1-eps)) [F_UU,T + eps F_UU,L + T_LL(F_UTLL,T + eps F_UTLL,L) + sqrt(2eps(1+eps)) T_LT cos(phi_TL) F_UTLT + eps T_TT cos(2phi_TT) F_UTTT]; the decomposition carries NO double-helicity-flip Delta term (their subject is b1).
Eq. (11c) eps = (1 - gamma^2 y^2/4)/(1 - y + y^2/2 + gamma^2 y^2/4); Eq. (13) gamma = M_d Q/(p_d.q) = 2 x_d M_d/Q; rescaled x = 2 x_d.
Eq. (14): in the deuteron rest frame with q along z, T_LL = t_zz, T_LT cos(phi_TL) = t_xz, T_TT cos(2phi_TT) = t_xx - t_yy (components of the polarization tensor).
Eq. (16): F_UU,L = (1+gamma^2) F2/x_d - 2 F1, F_UU,T = 2 F1.

Eq. (17): relations to HJM b1-b4. (17d) F_UTLT = -(gamma/2x_d)[(1+gamma^2)(b2/3 - b4) + 2b2/3 - 2b3] -> the cos(phi) tensor term is O(gamma). (17e) F_UTTT = -(gamma^2/x_d)(b2/6 - b3/2) -> the cos(2phi) tensor term from b2, b3 is O(gamma^2) (higher twist). Eq. (18) Callan-Gross-like b2 = 2 x_d b1 = x b1.

Eq. (20): axis along the virtual photon (N = N_q) -> T_LL = Q/3, T_LT = T_TT = 0 (only two tensor SFs enter: the clean choice for b1/A_zz). Eq. (22): axis along the electron beam (N = N_e) -> T_LL = (3cos^2 theta_q - 1)Q/6, T_LT cos(phi_TL) = -sin(2theta_q) Q/4, T_TT cos(2phi_TT) = (1 - cos 2theta_q) Q/4, theta_q = angle between q and the beam in the target rest frame.
Eqs. (25)-(27): Bjorken limit A_T = -(2/3) b1/F1 (the HERMES extraction relation). Reference gamma values: 0.66 at x = 0.5, Q2 = 2 GeV2; 0.30 at Q2 = 10 GeV2.
Fig. 6: at Q2 = 2 GeV2 the higher-twist b3, b4 are not negligible in the tensor asymmetry and are larger for polarization along the photon direction; they decrease with Q2.
Target context: JLab b1 experiment, DNP ND3 target, 5 T magnet with +-35 deg bore, longitudinal field planned; running with a longitudinal field creates theta_q != 0.
used_in: reports/reconstruction_chain_report.template.html section 2 (Harmonics from the tensor structure functions at finite gamma)

key_content: Eq. (1): Q2 y dsigma/(dQ2 dy dM2 dDelta2 dphi) = (alpha_em/2pi^2)[(1 - y + y^2/2) dsigma_T + (1-y) dsigma_L + (1-y) dsigma_TT cos(2phi) + (1 - y/2) sqrt(1-y) dsigma_LT cos(phi)] = ... key_content: Slide 40: inclusive kinematics from two of the four measured quantities D = {E_e, theta_e, delta_h, pT,h}, delta_h = sum_HFS E_i(1 - cos theta_i) (the E - p_z sum), pT,h the HFS transverse momentum; resolutions depend on the event's (x, Q2), detector acceptance/resolution, and radiative processes.

Slide 42 (ePIC 18x275 map, best method for y with marker size = y resolution 25/10/5/1%): electron method at high y, Sigma method in the middle, DA method along the y = 0.01 edge with ~25% markers; 'Resolution throughout phase space allowing 5 (log) bins per decade in x and Q2'; 'Coverage driven by acceptance: 0.01 < y < 0.95, Q2 > 1 GeV2'; 'Lower y accessible -> however it's easier to rely on overlap between data at different sqrt(s)'; 'No single method wins everywhere!'

Slide 43: Bayesian kinematic fit (KF) of all 4 measured quantities for lambda = {x, y, E_gamma} with a prior P0 ~ (1 + (1-y)^2)/(x^3 y^2) x (1 + (1 - E_gamma/E0)^2)/(E_gamma/E0); posterior by Metropolis-Hastings, global mode.

Slide 44 (smeared EIC pseudodata, Djangoh 18x275, Q2 > 1 GeV2): sigma(theta_e) = 0.1 mrad, sigma(E_e)/E = 11%/sqrt(E) (+) 2%, sigma(delta_h)/delta_h = 25%, sigma(pT,h)/pT,h = 25% (repo-verified 2026-08-25).

Slide 45: Delta y/y per method in y bins 0.01-0.05, 0.05-0.1, 0.1-0.2, 0.2-0.5, 0.5-0.8: in 0.01 < y < 0.05 the Sigma/JB/DA/KF methods give roughly Gaussian widths ~0.2-0.3 while the electron method is flat (unusable); at y > 0.2 the electron method and KF are narrowest.

Slide 47 (fully simulated ePIC, Pythia8 NC DIS, Craterlake 23.12.0, Q2 > 100 GeV2, electron from tracking, 0 <= eta <= 0.5): parametrized resolutions sigma_E = 0.055 p (+) 0.45 (Delta p/p in %, A p (+) B with A = 0.055, B = 0.45), sigma_theta = 72/pT (+) 2.8 mrad, sigma_delta_h = 0.25 delta_h, sigma_pT,h = 0.25 pT,h.

Slide 48: full ePIC simulation: 'KF gives comparable y resolution to electron method at high y; loses at low y to DA method'; in 0.01 < y < 0.05 DA is the narrowest, Sigma/JB broad with tails, electron flat. Slide 50: adding an HFS correlation term (width ~8%) recovers the KF at low y (comparable to DA).

Slide 51: ISR energy from the E - p_z conservation Sigma_total = 2E_e,beam (the relation implicit in the Sigma method); slides 52-56, 65: KF on H1 2003/04 data+MC (0.01 < y_eSigma < 0.6, Q2 > 200 GeV2) with sigma(theta_e) = 4 mrad, sigma(E_e)/E = 11%/sqrt(E) (+) 1%, sigma(delta_h)/delta_h = 13.5%, sigma(pT,h)/pT,h = 54%/sqrt(pT,h) (+) 4%; ISR energy reproduced within 30% for E_gamma > 3-4 GeV.

Slides 27-28, 37: ePIC tracking momentum and pointing resolution within reach of the Yellow Report targets except at the largest |eta|; backward momentum requirement still challenging ('high resolution EM calorimetry in this region may provide better reconstruction').

arratia2022-dnn-dis-kinematics.title: Reconstructing the Kinematics of Deep Inelastic Scattering with Deep Learning
key_content: Table 1: formulas of all classical methods from three of the five quantities {E0, E, theta, Sigma, gamma}: electron, DA, hadron (JB), ISigma, IDA, E0ESigma, E0thetaSigma, thetaSigmagamma, double energy (A4), ESigmaT, E0ET, Sigma, eSigma (Sigma = sum_HFS(E_i - p_z,i); Sigma_e the electron's E - p_z; T the HFS transverse momentum).

Setup: Rapgap 3.3 e+p at E0 = 18 GeV, Ep = 275 GeV through the Delphes fast simulation of ATHENA, restricted to Q2 > 200 GeV2; electron = highest-pT track with pT > 5 GeV, EM fraction > 0.8, isolation < 0.2; HFS from energy-flow candidates; Djangoh 1.4 for prior dependence; H1 full simulation (Rapgap 3.1, Geant3, HERA-II) for the demonstration.

Fig. 5 (ATHENA fast simulation, RMS of reco/gen vs generated y, ratio within 0-2): y resolution at y -> 0.05: electron ~0.3, hadron (JB) ~0.17, DA ~0.15, ISigma ~0.13, DNN ~0.05; at y = 0.2: electron ~0.10, DA/ISigma ~0.10, hadron ~0.17; x follows y at low y (electron ~0.3 at y -> 0.05); Q2 resolution: electron ~0.03-0.07, DA/ISigma ~0.05-0.1, hadron 0.15-0.35; the electron method's mean of y/y_gen is biased to 1.12 at the lowest y (repo read-off 2026-08-25).

Sec. 5 'Impact of further acceptance and resolution effects at low y': 'At low y, the HFS-based methods perform better than the electron method... the HFS momentum balance Sigma goes to zero as y goes to zero... Sigma at low y [is] especially sensitive to resolution effects or efficiency losses in the central part of the detector or fake components from calorimetric noise'; the Delphes fast simulation lacks calorimeter noise and edge effects; an ad-hoc Landau noise (mu = 0, sigma = 0.05 GeV per HFS momentum component) brings the fast simulation closer to the H1 full simulation at y <~ 0.15 (Fig. 11).

Fig. 8-9 (H1 full simulation): DNN yields the smallest RMS and is bias-free; at low y the DNN improves y and x substantially over electron and DA; the H1 selection required 45 < Sigma + Sigma_e < 65 GeV to suppress ISR.

abe1999-r1998-world-fit.title: Measurements of R = sigma_L/sigma_T for 0.03 < x < 0.1 and Fit to World Data
key_content: Eq. (2): THREE six-parameter forms, R1998 = their average ('As in the case of R1990, we define R1998 to be the average of the three fits'). R_a = a1 Theta/log(Q2/0.04) + a2 (Q^8 + a3^4)^(-1/4) [1 + a4 x + a5 x^2] x^a6; R_b = b1 Theta/log(Q2/0.04) + [b2/Q2 + b3/(Q^4 + 0.3^2)] [1 + b4 x + b5 x^2] x^b6; R_c = c1 Theta/log(Q2/0.04) + c2 [(Q2 - Q2thr)^2 + c3^2]^(-1/2) with Q2thr = c4 x + c5 x^2 + c6 x^3.  In the paper's notation Q^4 = (Q2)^2 and Q^8 = (Q2)^4; log is natural and 0.04 GeV2 = Lambda^2 (verified against the arXiv LaTeX source, 2026-08-26).

Eq. (3): Theta(x, Q2) = 1 + 12 [Q2/(Q2+1)] [0.125^2/(0.125^2 + x^2)].  Theta multiplies the log term of Eq. (2) and NOTHING ELSE.  Theta is 6.2-12.9 over x <= 0.05, 1 <= Q2 <= 130 (repo-measured; the code review's '6.5-9.5' is low), so putting it on all three terms saturates the sum: code review 2026-08-25 item S1, where the fast-sim money scripts' r1998 returns R = 1.000 over the whole low-x region.
Fit support: 237 points, 0.005 <= x <= 0.86 and 0.5 <= Q2 <= 130 GeV2 (paragraph above Eq. 2); confidence level 73% for all the data, 38% for x <= 0.07.

Fitting error, unnumbered equation below Eq. (3): delta-R(x,Q2) = 0.0078 - 0.013 x + (0.070 - 0.39 x + 0.70 x^2)/(1.7 + Q2).  The functional-form systematic is the spread of the three fits.  The paper's sentence 'This error is largest at low Q2, reaching a maximum value for x ~ 0.04' does not follow from that formula: d(delta-R)/dx = 0 at 1.4 x = 0.39 + 0.013 (1.7 + Q2), a MINIMUM at x = 0.299 for Q2 = 0.5 and x = 0.3408 for Q2 = 5, with no maximum anywhere in 0.005 <= x <= 0.86. At Q2 = 0.5 (repo-measured 2026-08-26) delta-R = 0.03867 at x = 0.005, 0.03252 at x = 0.04, 0.01117 at the x = 0.299 minimum and 0.11131 at x = 0.86. The formula is implemented as published; only the sentence is disputed.

Table I: E143 carbon cross sections and nine extracted values of R with stat and sys errors -- x, Q2 [GeV2], R: 0.0325, 1.32, 0.45 +- 0.01 +- 0.07; 0.0375, 1.47, 0.51 +- 0.02 +- 0.09; 0.0450, 1.67, 0.40 +- 0.01 +- 0.10; 0.0550, 1.90, 0.28 +- 0.01 +- 0.09; 0.0650, 2.11, 0.29 +- 0.02 +- 0.10; 0.0750, 2.29, 0.18 +- 0.02 +- 0.11; 0.0850, 2.46, 0.26 +- 0.03 +- 0.10; 0.0950, 2.60, 0.25 +- 0.03 +- 0.14; 0.1050, 2.73, 0.17 +- 0.03 +- 0.13. lee2024-snspd-120gev-proton-beam-test.title: Beam Tests of SNSPDs with 120 GeV Protons
key_content: The Argonne (MEP/Physics Division) device actually beam-tested: 12 nm NbN on a 300 um Si substrate, 30 x 30 um^2 active area per device with a fill factor of 1/2, 8 devices per 8 x 8 mm^2 chip. Wire widths 300, 400, 600 and 800 nm were fabricated; the paper's conclusion is that the wire width is the critical efficiency parameter and that widths above 400 nm lose efficiency at low bias -- ~250 nm is named as the ideal.

The number the whole Z-ID case rests on: the hot-spot radius. Their Eq. 1 r_s = sqrt(Q/(e pi c rho (Tc - T0))) and Eq. 2 detection criterion r_s / [(w/2)(1 - I_b/I_c)] >= 1 give the firing threshold I_th/I_c = 1 - 2 r_s / w. CAUTION: 134 nm is an EXTRAPOLATED zero-crossing, not a measurement -- the authors write 'While the physical validity of this simple model is a question of future work', and inverting their four points individually gives 102-118 nm (mean 113). Note also that Q here is 'the energy that the proton has deposited into the THIN FILM' (~20 eV), while arXiv:2601.03158 applies the same sqrt(Q) scaling to the SUBSTRATE deposit (0.1 MeV) -- a factor 5000 in what Q means; both scale as z^2, so r_s ~ z survives but the absolute radii do not. Fitting their threshold-vs-width points (~0.215 at 300 nm, 0.49 at 400, 0.62 at 600, 0.70 at 800) gives r_s = 134 nm for a 120 GeV proton, and the fit crosses zero at w ~ 268 nm -- hence their '~250 nm ideal'. Background counts rise exponentially above I_b/I_c > 0.8.
Operating point: T = 2.82 K in a Janis SHI-4 GM cryocooler (not a dilution or sorption fridge); film Tc ~ 7 K; Ic = 25.2 uA for the 400 nm device.
Beam: FTBF MT6.2, 120 GeV protons, ~10^6 protons/min in a 4.2 s spill. Background/signal measured to be (2.08 +/- 0.89)% -- i.e. essentially noise-free operation in a hadron beam.
Radiation hardness is explicitly NOT measured: characterization is stated as 'planned in the near future'. Any far-forward EIC application must treat the radiation tolerance as unmeasured.

Their own stated EIC motivation, which is exactly the far-forward aperture argument: 'Geometrical acceptance of semi-conductor detectors satisfying these requirements is limited by the beamline magnets, which can be mitigated by operating SNSPDs within the frigid bore of superconducting magnets.'
Corresponding author warmstrong@anl.gov (Argonne MEP group).

The decisive comparison this reference does NOT make, and which decides open question #19 against the technology (reports/nanowire_far_forward Sec. 4.1): a threshold nanowire yields ONE BIT per plane, while the incumbent ePIC AC-LGAD digitises an 8-bit charge over a 30 um active layer -- ~4.8 sigma of alpha/6Li separation per plane, over the four planes ePIC already has.
used_in: reports/nanowire_far_forward.template.html (the device baseline: 12 nm NbN film thickness sets the Z-ID energy deposits; 30 x 30 um^2 x 8 devices sets the tiling arithmetic; 2.82 K sets the cryostat class)

polakovic2019-snspd-high-magnetic-field.title: Superconducting nanowires as high-rate photon detectors in strong magnetic fields
key_content: The field-tolerance result the far-forward siting argument rests on: saturated internal efficiency is retained in fields PARALLEL to the device plane up to 5 T (the setup limit), with a conservative extrapolation to ~8 T; in PERPENDICULAR fields the practical limit is only ~0.5 T, past which dark counts from the near-critical state dominate. Orientation, not field magnitude, is the design constraint.
Device: NbN meander, 13.5 nm thick, 80 nm wide wires on 110 nm pitch, 10 x 10 um^2 pixel, grown by ion beam assisted sputtering. Tc = 8 K, Hc2(0) = 32 T, xi(0) = 3.2 nm, jC = 2.2e10 A/m^2.

Bias margin: saturated internal efficiency at ~9 uA against a critical current of 23 uA at zero field; at 5 T parallel, saturation at ~10 uA with dark-count onset at 12.5 uA -- the working margin narrows but survives.

Rate: 10^7 counts/s measured (limited by the LED heat load of the test setup, not the device); 10^8 counts/s expected from the 80-20% fall time tau_F = 11.78 +/- 1.6 ns, since rate ~ 1/tau_F. 20-80% rise time tau_R = 341 +/- 31 ps. Rate is raised by shortening the wire (lower L_K), shunting, or paralleling segments.
Operation at 3 K with negligible change at 4 K, and 'nearly zero dark counts' below the exponential onset.
used_in: reports/nanowire_far_forward.template.html (the parallel/perpendicular field asymmetry drives the sensor-plane orientation in the B1apf/B2apf region; the 10^8 /s rate ceiling sets the per-device occupancy budget)

wang2026-smspd-microwire-arrays.title: Towards High-Efficiency Particle Detection Using Superconducting Microwire Arrays
key_content: The large-area branch of the technology: an 8-channel 1 x 1 mm^2 WSi SMSPD array (pixel 0.125 x 1 mm^2) on a 4.7 nm W42Si58 film, 1 um wires on a 3 um gap. This is the answer to the SNSPD area problem -- mm^2 instead of the 100 um^2 of a nanowire device.

Price of the area: the fill factor is only 25% (1 um wire, 3 um gap) and the operating temperature is 0.8 K (PhotonSpot helium sorption fridge, ~30 h hold) against Tc = 1.85 K -- far colder than the 2.8-3 K NbN devices of arXiv:2312.13405 and 1907.13059.

Performance with 120 GeV hadrons and muons at CERN SPS H6, referenced to a 10 um silicon telescope: fill-factor-normalized detection efficiency ~75% and time resolution 130 +/- 17 ps, consistent across pixels and particle types. First SMSPD efficiency measurement for muons.
Improvement over the group's earlier 3 nm WSi / 1.5 um wire device: 60% -> 75% efficiency, 1.15 ns -> 130 ps time resolution. Thicker film, narrower wire.
used_in: reports/nanowire_far_forward.template.html (the area-versus-temperature trade: mm^2 SMSPD tiles vs 30 x 30 um^2 NbN devices, and the 25% fill factor that the geometric-efficiency budget must carry)

lee2026-cryogenic-test-station-alpha.title: Optimization of Cryogenic Detector Test Station by Rejecting Electromagnetic Interference
key_content: The second anchor of the hot-spot scaling, and the reason a relativistic 6Li is an INTERPOLATION rather than an extrapolation. Verbatim: 'The deposited energy forms a non-superconducting core of size proportional to the square root of the deposited energy. The previous work with a 120 GeV proton determined the hot spot size to be 134 nm, and a 5.5 MeV alpha particle creates an approximately 1 um hot spot by the same scaling.' A 6Li at 137.5 GeV/u lands at r_s ~ 400 nm, between their two points -- but in Q, NOT in z: this alpha differs from the 120 GeV proton almost entirely through 1/beta^2 (beta = 0.054 against ~1), so it calibrates sqrt(Q) across ENERGY and says nothing about z^2 at fixed velocity. Nobody has varied Z at fixed beta on one of these devices.
Devices: 12 nm NbN meanders, w in {100, 200, 300, 400} nm at d = 10 um and {100, 200, 400, 800} nm at d = 30 um, T = 2.7 K on a GM cryocooler. Source 241Am 100 uCi, alphas at 5.49/5.44/5.34 MeV.

Count-rate plateaus with NO latching: 2.5 +/- 0.3 Hz (100 nm, d = 10 um), 2.0 +/- 0.5 (200 nm, d = 10 um), 15.9 +/- 2.8 (200 nm, d = 30 um); the 30/10 um ratio 8.0 +/- 2.4 against a geometric 9. A ~1 um hot spot therefore does not latch a 100-200 nm wire.

The wire-width hint that Z-ID needs: 'the energy deposited by alpha particles is sufficient for detection in the 100 nm wire, which is narrower than the 250 nm devices optimal for 120 GeV proton detection'. But this is a STOPPING alpha, not a relativistic one, and the two mechanisms differ.

The alpha analysis itself is NOT published: 'While a detailed study of alpha detection is underway'. Low-bias operation needed an EMI-rejection scheme to see counts above the noise floor at all -- which is a caution for any 'bias the wire down until only Z = 3 fires' strategy.
used_in: reports/nanowire_far_forward.template.html (the second calibration point of r_s ~ sqrt(Q); the no-latching result; the readout-SNR caution on low-bias operation)

pena2025-smspd-2mm-array.title: Characterization of a Superconducting Microwire Single-Photon Detector Array for Charged-Particle Detection
key_content: The largest SMSPD array run in a GeV hadron beam: 8-channel 2 x 2 mm^2 WSi on a 3 nm film, 1.5 um wires with 2.25 um gaps (40% fill factor), pixels 0.25 x 2 mm^2. Spatial resolution 30 +/- 1 um for 120 GeV protons; time resolution 1.15 ns.

The measurement that kills pulse-height Z-ID: waveforms and amplitude distributions from 120 GeV protons, 8 GeV pions and 8 GeV showering electrons are indistinguishable, and 'the same amplitude threshold is used' for all. The amplitude is the diverted BIAS current, not the deposit. Charge information in this technology lives in the firing threshold and the wire width, never in the pulse height.
Together with arXiv:2510.11725 (4.7 nm film, 1 um wires, 75% efficiency, 130 ps) this is the area state of the art for particle detection: a few mm^2 with 8 channels.
used_in: reports/nanowire_far_forward.template.html (amplitude is binary -> Z-ID must be threshold-based; the area state of the art)

cloet2006-polarized-emc.title: Spin-dependent structure functions in nuclear matter and the polarized EMC effect
key_content: Eq. (23): R^{3/2 3/2}_{As} = polarized-to-naive ratio for a stretched J = 3/2 nucleus with the FULL spin-3/2 sum -- this is the definition plans/01:79 gives Delta R_A. Eq. (26): R^{(3/2 1)}_{As}, the alternative normalization. The two differ by up to 0.06 at x = 0.8.

FIG. 6 (page 7 of the arXiv PDF, upper-left panel): 7Li at Q^2 = 5 GeV^2, x in 0..1, ratio 0.6..1.2 -- blue dashed = unpolarized EMC effect, red solid = R^{(3/2 1)}_{As} (Eq. 26), red dotted = R^{3/2 3/2}_{As} (Eq. 23), 9Be points overlaid. DIGITIZED into fastsim/polli_fastsim/data/cbt_polemc_7Li_Q5.csv (see that directory's SOURCES.md).

The '2x' slogan: the ratio of EMC effects r(x) = (1 - R_pol)/(1 - R_unpol) is NOT a constant 2 -- on the digitized Eq.-23 curve it is 2.25 / 1.69 / 1.41 / 1.14 at x = 0.40 / 0.45 / 0.50 / 0.60 and falls below 1 above x ~ 0.65, where the two curves cross.
The polarized curve sits BELOW the unpolarized one at low x (0.927 vs 1.024 at x = 0.10) and above it at x > 0.8; the curves converge at x ~ 0.62-0.65.

tronchin2018-polarized-emc.title: Polarized EMC effect in the QMC model
key_content: Figure 4 (page 9 of the arXiv PDF): isospin-symmetric nuclear matter at Q^2 = 10 GeV^2, x in 0..1, ratio 0.6..1.2 -- blue solid = unpolarized EMC ratio, purple dashed = polarized (spin) EMC ratio. Both stop at x ~ 0.75. DIGITIZED into fastsim/polli_fastsim/data/tmt_polemc_nm_Q10.csv.

The QMC result: the polarized and unpolarized EMC effects are COMPARABLE, not a factor 2 apart. The digitized ratio-of-effects (1 - R_pol)/(1 - R_unpol) is 1.01 / 1.00 / 1.08 at x = 0.40 / 0.50 / 0.60, i.e. ~1 across the valence region, against CBT's 2.25 / 1.41 / 1.14.

Different target and scale from CBT (nuclear matter at Q^2 = 10 GeV^2 vs 7Li at Q^2 = 5 GeV^2), which is why the repository compares the two in the ratio-of-effects form applied to one common 7Li unpolarized baseline rather than subtracting the published R values.

cosyn2017-b1-convolution.title: Deuteron tensor structure function b1
key_content: FIG. 4 (page 9 of the arXiv PDF): x b1(x) at Q^2 = 2.5 GeV^2 -- theory 1 (blue) and theory 2 (green), each split into S-D interference (SD), D-D (DD) and their sum by dash pattern. DIGITIZED (the two sums) into fastsim/polli_fastsim/data/b1_cdks_q2p5.csv.

miller2014-b1-pion-hidden-color.title: Pionic and hidden-color, six-quark contributions to the deuteron b1 structure function
key_content: FIG. 5 (page 10 of the arXiv PDF): the total b1 = b1(pion) + b1(6q) that reproduces the HERMES data, single curve. DIGITIZED into fastsim/polli_fastsim/data/b1_miller.csv.
